newsitem.title: USA: U.S. markets not seen reacting to U.K. Labour win.
newsitem.headline: U.S. markets not seen reacting to U.K. Labour win.

text.p: Financial market participants in the U.S. had a muted reaction to the Labour party's overwhelming victory in the U.K. elections Thursday.
Labor party leader Tony Blair unseated Prime Minister John Major, ending 18 years of conservative rule in the U.K. But it meant little to the financial markets, said players here.

The consensus was that the bond, stock, and foreign exchange markets had already priced in a Labour victory. The fear was that the margin of victory would not have been sufficient to allow the party to govern effectively. But election results dispelled that on Thursday.
Thus, U.S. market professionals expected to see little reaction to Labour's win. Instead, they said the focus would be on how the party handles itself in coming months.
Observers expected to see a hike in interest rates by 25 basis points next week as the party would want to establish credibility quickly to stem inflation.

Gordon Brown, Labour's economic spokesman, was widely expected to be named Chancellor of the Exchequer and the faster he moved the more the markets would believe the government was serious on controlling inflation, they said.

Callum McCarthy, chief executive of Barclays De Zoete Wedd Securities Inc in the U.S., said that regardless of which party won, a quick move to raise interest rates was expected in the markets. The sooner a new government moved to do so the more credibility it would have, he said.
McCarthy said the size of Labour win ended worries that a hung parliament would be seated, unable to effectively get legislation passed. That, he said, was "quite good" for bonds and sterling.

A potential problem could exist for equities down the road as a possible tax on windfall corporate taxes has been discussed and it was unclear as to which corporations would be affected -- but the utility sector has been targeted, analysts said.

"U.K. institutions are sitting on the highest cash levels they've had in six or seven years. The bond market certainly won't run away with itself," said Tony Gould, senior vice president at Fiduciary Trust Co. International.
Gould said regardless of which party won, the government was constrained by the financial markets and international investors currently were comfortable with the U.K.
Recent changes in the Canadian and Italian governments largely were ignored, he said, as investors ignored ideological slants of the new political regimes.
Ben Kottler, investment manager at Brown Brothers Harriman, also saw a 25 basis point hike in the base rate, but wouldn't be surprised by a 50-point increase.

"The equity market has priced this (Labour victory) in. There may even be a relief rally, but worries persist in the utilities sector as (the government ) hasn't been specific about which companies it would target and for how much," Kottler said.
Kottler said the overall British economy was in good shape, but as when U.S. President Bill Clinton was elected, a lot of people in the U.K. didn't believe that to be true.

Marshall Millsap, director of network management at Chase Bank, said the markets had discounted a Labour party victory into prices for some time. Few specific promises had been made, however, and they now would have to fill in the gaps.

The margin of the Labour win suggested to economists that two terms in office were likely as the Conservatives would be hard-pressed to rebound before new elections. That suggested stability and the financial markets likely would dwell on that as a calming factor, they said.
Oliver Grieves, a vice president at Metropolitan Life, and a British ex-patriate said the "new" Labour party had assured that no radical changes were in the making.
"My friends and family were all concerned about the snafus in U.K. politics. They were just tired of the mistakes the Conservative party has made," he said.
